title: Chore Chart for Teenagers (Free Printable + Money)
meta_description: A free printable chore chart for teenagers, with an optional allowance column. Real, honest advice from a dad of four on what actually works at 15.
h1: Chore Chart for Teenagers: Free Printable With an Optional Money Column
intro: If you came here looking for a chore chart for teenagers, you already know teens are a different animal than little kids. Stickers don't move them, and a chart taped to the fridge can feel a little kindergarten by the time someone's fifteen. We get it. In our house we're raising four kids, ages nine to eighteen, and our middle daughter is fifteen right now, so this is the exact stage we're living. The chart below is built for an older teen: real responsibilities, no cartoon icons, and an optional money/allowance column you can switch on. Generate it, print it, and use it as a tracking tool, not a bribe. We'll be honest below about how we actually run this with our own teenagers, including the part where the chart starts to fade and something more grown-up takes its place.

sections.heading: What a 15-Year-Old Can Realistically Handle
sections.body: By fifteen, a teen can run most of a household task start to finish without supervision, and that's the bar we hold to. A fifteen-year-old can cook a simple meal, do their own laundry from hamper to drawer, load and unload the dishwasher, take care of trash and recycling, keep their room and a shared space clean, and pitch in on bigger jobs like yard work or helping a parent with a repair. The shift from the younger years isn't really about adding more boxes to a chart. It's about quality and follow-through: doing the job well, and doing it without three reminders. That's why this chart drops the picture icons and keeps the language plain. At this age the chart's real value is letting you see, at a glance, who's actually carrying their weight, so you know when to step in and when to leave it alone.

sections.heading: How We Actually Run It (and Why the Chart Becomes a Parent Tool)
sections.body: Here's the honest part. With our teens, the daily chore chart gets hard to enforce, and we found that fighting it line by line wasn't worth it. The chart still earns its place, but its job changes: it's there for us to track how each kid is doing, not to nag the kid. The way we frame chores hasn't changed since they were small. We all contribute because we're a family, not because there's a prize at the end. That expectation does the motivating, not the chart. We also keep rewards and consequences separate from the chores themselves. We don't make our teens work to earn screen time, and we don't bribe them with it either. Losing screen time is a consequence for a behavior problem, not a chore currency. Keeping those two things apart has saved us a lot of arguments, because chores stop being a negotiation and just become part of how the house runs.

sections.heading: The Optional Money Column: How We Handle Allowance With Teens
sections.body: This chart has a money/allowance column you can turn on, and it's useful for tracking, but we'd steer you away from paying per task. In our house the teen setup looks more like a job than a chore list. Our teenagers get a set amount each month (we landed on $75) and that money is for wants, like grabbing Starbucks with friends, never for needs, which we cover. The money isn't tied to individual checkboxes. It's tied to the whole picture: quality of work, consistency, and attitude. With that monthly amount comes the understanding that we can ask them to take on agreed jobs ahead of time, babysitting a sibling, cooking, a deep clean. If tasks get skipped or forgotten, the amount gets trimmed at month-end. If the follow-through really falls apart, the money pauses until they show a couple of solid weeks and earn it back. So use the money column to keep score if you like, but think of it as a base tied to follow-through, not a price tag on the dishes.

faq.q: What chores should a 15-year-old be responsible for?
faq.a: By fifteen a teen can handle nearly any household task on their own: cooking simple meals, doing their own laundry, dishes, trash and recycling, keeping their room and shared spaces clean, and helping with yard work or repairs. At this age the goal shifts from learning the task to doing it well and without reminders.

faq.q: Should I pay my teenager for chores?
faq.a: We don't pay per chore. In our house teens get a set monthly amount (we use $75) that's for wants, not needs, and it's gated on quality, consistency, and attitude rather than individual tasks. Skipped jobs trim it at month-end. Treat the chart's money column as a way to track follow-through, not a per-task price.

faq.q: How do I get a teenager to actually do chores?
faq.a: Motivation comes from the expectation, not the chart. We frame it as we all contribute because we're a family, and we keep rewards and screen time separate from chores so nothing becomes a negotiation. With our teens the chart mostly becomes a tracking tool for us, a way to see who's carrying their weight and when to step in.

faq.q: Is a chore chart still worth using for teenagers?
faq.a: Yes, but its job changes. For little kids the chart guides them; for teens it's mostly there for the parents, letting you see at a glance how each kid is doing and decide when to intervene. Print it without icons, keep the language adult, and use it to track rather than to nag.
